blurb: A load balancer decides which server gets each request, and that one decision sets how long users wait.
Retries feel safe, but when many clients retry at once they keep a system overloaded long after the fault is gone.
Two full copies of production: deploy to the idle one, flip all traffic with one switch, keep the old one ready.
An index is a sorted copy of a few columns that points back to the rows: fast lookups, paid for on every write.
How a list API remembers where the last page ended decides how fast deep pages are and whether rows repeat or vanish.
Concurrency is one worker juggling many tasks by switching between them. It hides waiting but adds no extra hands.
Parallelism is many pieces of work at the same instant. More workers help only as far as the work can be split.
Async I/O lets one worker start many slow operations and handle each result when it's ready, instead of waiting.
JavaScript runs your code on one thread, one task at a time. Timers, network replies and drawing all wait their turn.
Two requests read the same value, both write, and one quietly undoes the other. Nothing crashes, so it hides.
Broadcast means every node learns every value; the topology decides how many messages that costs and how long it takes.
Every round, whoever knows tells a few random others. Nobody coordinates, nothing is retried, and everyone hears it fast.
A log keeps records in arrival order and doesn't delete them on read; each consumer group keeps a bookmark instead.
Counting sounds trivial until several machines count at once: lost updates, retries, and counters that never conflict.
Readiness asks “can you take traffic now?”, liveness asks “do you need a restart?” Mix them up and blips become outages.
Save to the database and tell other services in two writes, and a crash between them loses or invents events.
A lost reply makes the client pay again. An idempotency key lets the server spot the retry and replay the result.
Flight, hotel, car, card: no shared transaction, so when a late step fails a saga undoes the earlier ones in reverse.
One query for the list, then one per row. Each is a round trip, so it's invisible locally and slow in staging.
When a hot cache entry expires, every request misses at once and the database takes the whole herd.
Connections are slow to open and the database holds few. Most pool trouble is sizing, leaks and holding one too long.
Every metric label multiplies the series you store, and every trace costs space, so what you record must be chosen.
Wait until events stop, then act once. Every keystroke restarts the wait, so a burst becomes one request.
Run the handler at most once per interval while events keep coming: steady updates during a scroll, the rest dropped.
First in, first out. Between producers and workers a queue soaks up bursts and survives crashes, if you ack right.
Last in, first out: every function call, every undo, and under overload, which users still get an answer in time.
